title: Oral Reading Fluency Assessments: What the Data Is Missing
author: Michelle Ruhe
summary: Literacy coach Michelle Ruhe asks why a stack of Oral Reading Fluency (ORF) results so rarely tells teachers what to do next. Her answer is that the standard ORF only counts missed words in one minute, so it says little about the strategies a child controls, how well they comprehend, or whether vocabulary and background knowledge are the barrier. She walks through four typical scenarios, from the fast accurate reader to the struggling one, showing that the prescribed next steps leave comprehension largely a guess. Rather than adding yet another assessment to teachers' workloads, she recommends squeezing more from the ORF already being given. Her upgrades are to keep a true running record that notes error types, self-corrections and insertions, to capture phrasing and expression, and to let the child finish the passage and retell it so that a snapshot of comprehension emerges.
points: A standard ORF records only missed words per minute, so it cannot reveal strategy use, comprehension or the causes of errors.
Existing comprehension options such as MAZE, Acadience CFOL, Cubed-3 or whole-book kits are either narrow, training-heavy or too slow and costly for most classrooms.
Converting the ORF into a running record exposes the kinds of errors a child makes, including insertions that many protocols wrongly ignore.
Noting phrasing, punctuation and expression turns the fluency check into richer diagnostic information.
Letting the child finish the text and then retell it gives a quick, informal view of which parts they understood.
quotes: Well, often because the data is missing key pieces of the information we need in order to get started on next steps. The information we do have usually tells us a brief overview of skills, but it does not tell us the other important pieces we need.

Its purpose is to quickly gauge how accurately and fluently a child can read what is considered a “grade level” text. The assumption is that if they can read it smoothly and accurately, it is likely that the child can also comprehend any text they read. Which may or may not be true.
As students read for one minute, teachers are to cross off when an error is made–substitutions, mispronunciations, or omissions. Insertions, oddly, are not counted as errors.

So…not a whole lot of options that are actually accessible, helpful, doable, or don’t take a ton of time. Which takes us right back to the original problem: we need more useful information, not more assessments.

Recording what a child’s attempts are, whether they reread, sound out, or appeal for help gives you something to go on. Simply crossing out words a child missed will never give you this kind of critical information.

Many ORF tests don’t ask teachers to count insertions as errors. These are absolutely errors, often caused by reading too quickly and then trying to make the text grammatically or semantically sensible.
These assessments are not designed to gauge comprehension, but we can capture a snapshot of it. In terms of quick and informal, it will at least tell you if the child understood what they read/heard.

At the end of the day, we need to understand more than just how many words a child can read in a minute. In order to make next-step instructional decisions, we need to understand what students already know how to do as readers and where they get stuck.
context: The problem she names is that fluency data leaves out the information teachers need to choose a next step.
She sets out what ORF is built to measure and flags the unproven assumption that fluent readers comprehend.
The scoring rules capture only a narrow slice of the child's reading, and even skip insertions.
She concludes that the available alternatives are impractical, so teachers need better use of existing data.
Her first fix is a running record that shows how a child attempts words, not only which ones were missed.
She explains why insertions deserve to be recorded as errors, since they trace back to earlier mistakes.
Her second fix is a quick retell, which gives teachers an informal comprehension snapshot from the same text.
The closing claim is that instruction should rest on what students can already do and where they stall.
